chapters.title: Proverbs 1
body: This book opens naming its purpose plainly: to know wisdom and instruction, to give discretion to the young and simple. Then wisdom herself is personified, crying aloud in the streets, at the gates, in the busiest public places — not hidden in a temple requiring a pilgrimage, but shouting where ordinary people actually walk.

Wisdom's warning is sharp: those who refuse her now will eventually call and "I will not answer... because they hated knowledge." This isn't cruelty; it's naming a real pattern — habitual refusal eventually closes a door that was, for a long time, standing wide open. If wisdom has been calling to you in some ordinary, unglamorous place lately, this chapter suggests that's exactly where she's meant to be heard.

chapters.title: Proverbs 2
body: Wisdom here is described as something actively pursued, not passively received: "if thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures." It requires the same focused effort people give to things they genuinely value, not a casual hope that understanding will simply arrive.

The reward described isn't abstract — it includes protection from "the way of evil" and from "the strange woman," a specific, concrete kind of discernment that can tell a flattering, dangerous path from a genuinely good one. If you've wondered whether wisdom is something you passively wait for or actively dig toward, this chapter answers clearly: dig like it's treasure, because it is.

chapters.title: Proverbs 3
body: "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding" is this chapter's most famous line, but it's immediately followed by something practical: "in all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths." Trust here isn't just a feeling — it's a habit of consulting God in the actual decisions of daily life.

The chapter also instructs honoring God "with the firstfruits of all thine increase," and names discipline from God as something to be received rather than despised, "for whom the LORD loveth he correcteth." If being corrected has ever felt only like rejection, this chapter frames it instead as a specific sign of being genuinely loved, not written off.

chapters.title: Proverbs 4
body: This father recalls his own father's instruction, creating a visible chain: a father who was once a son, passing on what he himself received. "Get wisdom, get understanding" is urged with real urgency, framed as the most important acquisition of a lifetime, worth more than anything else being pursued.

"Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life" treats the heart not as a vague feeling-center but as the actual wellspring everything else flows from. If you've focused effort on controlling your actions while neglecting the deeper source of them, this chapter redirects the real work toward guarding that source first.

chapters.title: Proverbs 5
body: This chapter warns specifically against the "strange woman" whose lips "drop as an honeycomb," but whose end is "bitter as wormwood" — a deliberate contrast between immediate sweetness and eventual, serious cost. The warning is pointed and physical: wasted years, strength given to strangers, a ruined reputation "full of heaviness."

The chapter's constructive answer isn't just restraint but redirected delight: "rejoice with the wife of thy youth... let her be as the loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy thee at all times." The counsel isn't only to avoid the wrong thing — it's to actively cultivate real delight in the right one, so the wrong one loses its pull by comparison.

chapters.title: Proverbs 6
body: This chapter pivots through several distinct dangers: foolish financial surety for a stranger, laziness (pointing to the ant, who "provideth her meat in the summer" with no overseer required), and a vivid list of "seven things" God hates, ending with "he that soweth discord among brethren." The ant is a small, almost humorous example used to make a serious point about self-motivated diligence.

The chapter returns to the adulteress with blunt physical language: "can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned?" The imagery is deliberately uncomfortable, meant to make the danger viscerally obvious rather than abstractly understood. If a tempting choice has started to feel safely manageable in your own mind, this chapter's fire imagery is a reminder that some risks were never actually containable.

chapters.title: Proverbs 7
body: This chapter tells a short, deliberately detailed story: a young man, specifically "void of understanding," wandering near a tempting corner "in the twilight," meeting a woman dressed and perfumed for the encounter, who flatters him with smooth words and a bed "perfumed with myrrh." The specificity isn't incidental — it shows exactly how temptation actually arrives.

"He goeth after her straightway, as an ox goeth to the slaughter" names the terrifying ordinariness of it — no dramatic villain, just an unprepared person walking into exactly the wrong place at exactly the wrong time. If you've wondered whether staying out of certain places and times matters as much as resisting temptation directly, this chapter argues the former is often the real battleground.

chapters.title: Proverbs 8
body: Wisdom speaks in her own voice here, extensively and confidently: "by me kings reign," riches and honor are hers to give, and she declares she was present "when he prepared the heavens... when he appointed the foundations of the earth," rejoicing "before him" at creation's very beginning. This is some of the Bible's boldest personification, wisdom not just a quality but almost a figure present with God from eternity.

"I was by him, as one brought up with him: and I was daily his delight, rejoicing always before him" describes creation itself as something joyful, not merely functional. If you've thought of wisdom as a dry, serious virtue, this chapter's vivid, joyful self-portrait of wisdom offers something far livelier.

chapters.title: Proverbs 9
body: This chapter pictures two women issuing competing invitations: Wisdom, who has built a house, prepared a feast, and sends servants to call the simple to "come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine," offering real nourishment and life. Folly sits at her own door, loud and simple, offering stolen bread and water that seems sweet but leads, unnamed to her guests, toward death.

Both women use nearly identical language — "whoso is simple, let him turn in hither" — making the real difference entirely about what's actually being offered beneath similar-sounding invitations. If two paths in front of you right now sound equally appealing on the surface, this chapter suggests looking past the invitation itself to what each one is actually leading toward.

chapters.title: Proverbs 10
body: This chapter opens the book's long middle section — mostly short, standalone proverbs rather than a continuous argument — starting with a personal, domestic observation: "a wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish son is the heaviness of his mother." Even this section's abstract-sounding wisdom keeps returning to concrete, ordinary relationships.

"He that gathereth in summer is a wise son: but he that sleepeth in harvest is a son that causeth shame" uses an agricultural image everyone in that culture would immediately recognize — wisdom isn't exotic knowledge, but attentiveness to timing that ordinary life already requires. These proverbs reward being read slowly, one at a time, rather than skimmed as a single block.

chapters.title: Proverbs 11
body: "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight" opens this chapter with commerce, of all things — ordinary business transactions treated as a genuine moral and spiritual matter. Honesty in weighing goods isn't a side issue to real faith; it's one of its concrete, measurable expressions.

"He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him: but blessing shall be upon the head of him that selleth it" ties generosity directly to how someone handles scarcity for profit, not just how they feel about the poor in the abstract. If you've compartmentalized your faith away from your actual business or financial dealings, this chapter insists they were never meant to be separate.

chapters.title: Proverbs 12
body: "Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish" measures spiritual maturity by a specific, testable reaction: how someone actually responds to being corrected, not by how much they already know. A person can know a great deal and still fail this exact test.

"A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed is as rottenness in his bones" describes relational influence in bodily, visceral terms — something as central to someone's wellbeing as their own skeleton, not a peripheral matter. These proverbs keep insisting character shows up in exactly how it's received, not just how it's intended.

chapters.title: Proverbs 13
body: "He that keepeth his mouth keepeth his life: but he that openeth wide his lips shall have destruction" treats self-controlled speech as literally life-preserving, not merely polite. Several proverbs in this chapter circle the same theme from different angles — restrained words, honest words, patient words — suggesting the tongue is one of wisdom's most frequently tested areas.

"The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing: but the soul of the diligent shall be made fat" draws a sharp line between wanting and actually doing, a distinction this whole book keeps returning to. Desire alone, however sincere, isn't treated here as equivalent to the diligence that actually produces something.

chapters.title: Proverbs 14
body: "Every wise woman buildeth her house: but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands" opens with a vivid, active image — foolishness isn't passive, it's a demolition carried out by one's own hands, often in the same ordinary place wisdom would have built something lasting instead. The home becomes a concrete test case for both wisdom and folly.

"Where no oxen are, the crib is clean: but much increase is by the strength of the ox" names a real tradeoff: avoiding the mess of real productivity keeps things tidy but also keeps things empty. If you've chosen the cleaner, emptier option to avoid the inconvenience real growth requires, this proverb names exactly that quiet trade and asks whether it's actually worth it.

chapters.title: Proverbs 15
body: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger" opens with one of the book's most practical, testable claims about conflict — the same disagreement can escalate or de-escalate depending almost entirely on tone, not just content. This single sentence has settled more arguments than most elaborate conflict-resolution theories.

"The eyes of the LORD are in every place, beholding the evil and the good" grounds all these practical sayings in something larger: not just useful advice for getting along, but an awareness of being seen everywhere, all the time. If gentler speech has ever felt like simply avoiding conflict rather than genuinely resolving it, this chapter treats a soft answer as real strength, not avoidance dressed up as virtue.

chapters.title: Proverbs 16
body: "The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD" opens this chapter with a humbling observation: even our planning and our speech depend on God in ways we don't fully control ourselves. "Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established" follows, pointing toward partnership rather than either pure self-reliance or passive waiting.

"A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps" captures this tension precisely — real human planning, and real divine direction operating alongside it, neither canceling the other out. If you've wondered how much of your own life to plan versus simply surrender, this chapter suggests both belong together rather than being opposite postures.

chapters.title: Proverbs 17
body: "Better is a dry morsel, and quietness therewith, than an house full of sacrifices with strife" compares modest peace favorably against abundance soured by conflict — a direct challenge to the assumption that more resources automatically mean more wellbeing. The quality of relationships, this proverb insists, matters more than the volume of provisions.

"Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker" ties disrespect toward the vulnerable directly back to disrespect toward God himself, since the poor person is also made in his image. "Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise" closes with a reminder that silence, well-timed, can sometimes communicate more wisdom than speech ever could.

chapters.title: Proverbs 18
body: "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him" offers a sober warning about hearing only one side of a conflict before forming a judgment — the first account always sounds reasonable until a second one arrives to complicate it. "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame to him" states this even more bluntly.

"The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom as a flowing brook" compares genuine wisdom to something continually flowing, not a stagnant pool drawn down once and exhausted. "A man's gift maketh room for him" and "a friend that sticketh closer than a brother" round out a chapter deeply concerned with how words and relationships actually function in daily life.

chapters.title: Proverbs 19
body: "Better is the poor that walketh in his integrity, than he that is perverse in his lips, and is a fool" directly challenges any assumption that status matters more than character — integrity without wealth is named here as genuinely better than cleverness without honesty. "Wealth maketh many friends; but the poor is separated from his neighbour" names, without approval, a sad social reality worth noticing rather than accepting as right.

"He that hath mercy on the poor, happy is he" and "he that spareth his rod hateth his son" sit side by side, showing this book's wisdom as both tender and firm depending on what the moment genuinely requires. "Hear counsel, and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end" closes with a long view: wisdom gained now pays off specifically later, not necessarily right away.

chapters.title: Proverbs 20
body: "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise" opens a chapter naming specific vulnerabilities plainly — not abstract moral theory, but concrete warnings about particular behaviors that genuinely derail a life. "The sluggard will not plow by reason of the cold; therefore shall he beg in harvest, and have nothing" draws a direct line from a small avoidable discomfort now to real poverty later.

"It is an honour for a man to cease from strife: but every fool will be meddling" names restraint from unnecessary conflict as genuine strength, not weakness. "Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD" returns once more to honest commerce — a recurring theme this book clearly considers central, not incidental, to real integrity.

chapters.title: Proverbs 21
body: "The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will" names something comforting and unsettling at once: even the most powerful human authority is, ultimately, not beyond God's reach. "Every way of a man is right in his own eyes: but the LORD pondereth the hearts" warns against trusting your own self-assessment too confidently.

"The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want" contrasts patient, steady effort against impulsive haste, a theme this book returns to constantly. "To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice" insists that ethical action, not religious performance alone, is what God actually values most.

chapters.title: Proverbs 22
body: "A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold" opens the chapter ranking reputation and relationship above material wealth outright. "The rich and poor meet together: the LORD is the maker of them all" levels economic distinction before the one fact that outranks it — shared origin from the same Maker.

"Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it" is often quoted as an ironclad guarantee, but it's better read as a general pattern within a book of general wisdom sayings, not a formula without exception. "Remove not the old landmark; and enter not into the fields of the fatherless" protects the vulnerable against quiet, gradual encroachment on what's theirs — the kind of theft that happens slowly enough to go unnoticed.

chapters.title: Proverbs 23
body: "Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom. Wilt thou set thine eyes upon that which is not? for riches certainly make themselves wings; they fly away as an eagle toward heaven" names wealth's fundamental instability — it's never actually as secure or substantial as it looks while you're chasing it.

This chapter also contains one of the Bible's most direct statements on discipline: "withhold not correction from the child... thou shalt deliver his soul from hell." And it returns, pointedly, to the danger of drunkenness, describing its physical and relational wreckage in vivid, specific detail — "thine eyes shall behold strange women, and thine heart shall utter perverse things" — a warning meant to be felt, not merely understood intellectually.

chapters.title: Proverbs 24
body: "Be not thou envious against evil men, neither desire to be with them" opens a warning against admiring the wrong kind of success, since surface prosperity can hide a heart "studying destruction." "Through wisdom is an house builded; and by understanding it is established" repeats this book's favorite metaphor — wisdom isn't abstract, it's what actually holds a household together, room by room.

"If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small" is honest about the fact that real character shows most clearly under genuine pressure, not in easy seasons. The chapter closes watching a field "grown over with thorns," a sluggard's untended ground left to decay — a vivid, unglamorous picture of what neglect, unchecked, actually produces over time.

chapters.title: Proverbs 25
body: "It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter" opens a new section, copied out by Hezekiah's men generations after Solomon, showing wisdom itself was actively preserved and passed down, not left to chance. "Take away the dross from the silver, and there shall come forth a vessel for the finer" uses refining as a metaphor for removing corrupt influence before anything lasting can actually be built.

"If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink" is a startling instruction that anticipates the New Testament's call to love enemies, centuries early. "As cold waters to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country" captures something ordinary and universally recognizable — the specific relief of hearing that someone far away is actually okay.

chapters.title: Proverbs 26
body: This chapter offers a famous paradox back to back: "answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him" is immediately followed by "answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit." Wisdom here isn't a single rigid rule — it's discerning which approach a given moment actually calls for, since the same advice can be right or wrong depending on context.

"As a door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed" and "as the dog returneth to his vomit, so a fool returneth to his folly" use blunt, almost comic images to make serious points about laziness and repeated bad choices land harder than abstract moralizing ever could.

chapters.title: Proverbs 27
body: "Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth" names a real limit on human certainty, worth remembering before any confident plan. "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful" distinguishes real friendship from flattery by what it's actually willing to risk saying, not by how pleasant it sounds in the moment.

"Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend" pictures genuine friendship as something that actively improves a person, through friction as much as comfort. "As in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man" suggests people genuinely reflect each other — who you spend time with shapes who you actually become, a theme this book returns to again and again.

chapters.title: Proverbs 28
body: "The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion" compares guilt's inner anxiety against the quiet confidence that comes from an honest conscience — the real pursuer, often, is someone's own unresolved wrongdoing, not an actual outside threat. "Whoso covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy" states this directly without hedging.

"He that giveth unto the poor shall not lack: but he that hideth his eyes shall have many a curse" returns once more to care for the poor as a central, repeated test of genuine character, not a peripheral virtue. "A poor man that oppresseth the poor" is named specifically as an especially ugly failure — mistreatment isn't excused just because the person doing it is also struggling.

chapters.title: Proverbs 29
body: "He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy" names a real pattern — not one bad decision, but a repeated refusal to adjust after correction, which eventually closes off the option to fix things at all. "When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn" measures leadership honestly by its actual effect on ordinary people's daily experience.

"The king by judgment establisheth the land: but he that receiveth gifts overthroweth it" names corruption's specific mechanism — not abstract wickedness, but concrete bribery that quietly dismantles a whole system's fairness. "The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe" offers a real alternative to living primarily to manage other people's opinions.

chapters.title: Proverbs 30
body: Agur's words open with startling humility for a wisdom book: "surely I am more brutish than any man, and have not the understanding of a man." He then asks a series of unanswerable questions about God's nature — who has gathered the wind, bound the waters, established the earth — admitting real limits to human knowledge rather than performing false mastery.

The chapter's numerical sayings — "there be three things... yea, four" — observe nature with genuine delight and curiosity: the way of an eagle, a serpent on a rock, a ship on the sea. Wisdom here includes honest wonder and admitted ignorance alongside confident instruction, a humility this whole book rarely states so explicitly.

chapters.title: Proverbs 31
body: This final chapter opens with a mother's instruction to her son, King Lemuel — advice against wasting strength on women and wine, and a striking command instead to "open thy mouth for the dumb... judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy." Royal character, in her teaching, is measured by advocacy for people with no voice of their own.

The chapter's famous acrostic then describes a capable woman in vivid, active, entirely unsentimental detail: she works with willing hands, considers a field and buys it, her candle doesn't go out at night, she stretches out her hand to the poor, she speaks wisdom, she laughs at the time to come. "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised" closes both this chapter and the whole book — thirty-one chapters of wisdom ending not in abstraction, but in one specific, fully realized, flourishing life.
